item.title: How Do You Help a Child With ADHD Be Happy?
item.description:
ADHD

How Do You Help a Child With ADHD Be Happy?

Kids with ADHD can flourish by focusing on strengths and addressing challenges.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Predictable challenges for children with ADHD can be addressed with different fixes.
  • Strengths exhibited by people with ADHD include zest, vitality, optimism, energy and cognitiive flexibility.
  • Focusing on strengths, sports, music and nature helps kids with ADHD flourish.

Ask any parent what they want for their child, and most will give the same answer: happiness. But how exactly can you help a child with ADHD grow into a happy, self-sufficient adult?

With personal stories, evidence-based approaches, and recommended skills to implement in your own life, my new book, Our Guide to Navigating ADHD: How to Embrace Challenges, Develop Grit, and Flourish, offers guidance on how to help your child move from floundering to flourishing.

In 2024, the CDC estimated that 7 million children ages 3-17 will be diagnosed with ADHD in childhood.

Although children living with ADHD have very real challenges, it is possible to find ways to address and move past them. Some of the challenges are: decreased life expectancy; illicit drug and alcohol use; sleep disorders; accidental injuries; justice system involvement; low income and unemployment; difficulty finding positive peers; and suffering the judgment of other parents. Each of these challenges has a corresponding “fix”: developing good habits of exercise, healthy eating and getting enough sleep; embrace a course of medication prescribed by a qualified health provider; lock up dangerous things like guns; use the American Academy of Pediatrics’ Family Media Plan to help plan when and what to view; hold your child accountable for infraction of rules; support school personnel in administering consequences; figure out how to cover educational expenses so that students can begin employment debt-free; enroll children in sports; and practice ignoring what others say about you and your child.

There are positive traits associated with ADHD too. People with ADHD often have increased zest and vitality compared with others. They are full of energy and exhibit humor and optimism. Cognitive flexibility, or being able to see a situation from several angles at once, can be useful in addressing difficult logistical problems.

Focusing on strengths is a great place to start. Think about all of the things about your child that are positive in these spheres: individual, family, school, peers, neighborhood community. Now, which can be harder, begin to realize that even when disobeying or not able to control impulses, a child with ADHD can exhibit these strengths. Beginning to focus on the strengths in the presence of other behaviors lays a foundation for helping children with ADHD learn to regulate their behavior.

A 2025 CDC report says that most children (about 61%) ages 6 to 17 years are flourishing. Children with ADHD had been found to be flourishing but at lower rates (about 25%), as reported by caregivers. What does that mean? The National Survey of Children’s Health (NSCH) includes the following items to define flourishing for children: bounces back quickly when things don’t go their way; shows curiosity in learning new things; stays calm when faced with a challenge; works to finish a task they start. It is easy to see why children with ADHD might not exhibit these behaviors as frequently as other children. Dr. Martin Seligman has proposed the acronym PERMA to describe flourishing: Positive emotions; Engagement; Relationships; Meaning; and Accomplishments. These trends are easier to see in older children or adults, but we can draw the throughline from the NSCH items.

Thinking about how to enhance flourishing among children with ADHD, it can help to think about how to address barriers. These include executive function deficits like working memory; emotional regulation; self-motivation and time management. Fortunately, three developmentally appropriate disciplines can address these: sports, music and nature, which will be discussed more in a future post. Research in each of these areas shows that, when children with ADHD engage in them over a period of time, their symptoms can improve. In addition, they can gain self-efficacy and develop relationships with positive peers who are involved in the same activities.

item.title: Optimism and Pessimism Are Contrasting Worldviews
item.description:
Pessimism

Optimism and Pessimism Are Contrasting Worldviews

Optimists have more internal harmony while pessimists have more discord.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Optimists and pessimists have different degrees of internal harmony and balance.
  • Optimism tends to cause a person to expand their connections to themself, other persons, and the world.
  • Pessimism tends to cause people to shrink their worlds, running the risk of their worlds collapsing.
  • William James offers a robust description of how a pessimist is vulnerable to "pathological melancholy."

What are the differences between optimists and pessimists? While there are some stark differences between the two types of people, it turns out that each of us is often a mixture of optimism and pessimism. The balance can shift many times over a lifetime. Many who presently are struggling with addiction and those in recovery may recognize how this balance shifts. So, too, will those who have struggled with acute or chronic anguish.

Meet the optimists

Optimists and pessimists differ significantly in the degree of unity and harmony within their own person and with the broader world. According to William James (1842-1910), we human beings have multiple selves or aspects that can be harmonious or discordant. Each person has material, social, and spiritual dimensions.

  • The material dimensions include our bodies, family members, clothes, and prized or hard-earned possessions such as a house.
  • Our social selves are a matter of our actual or imagined relations to others. Each of us is someone’s child, friend, co-worker, community member, neighbor, for example. We have as many social selves as people who recognize us.
  • Our spiritual selves, James claims, are the locus of our interests and efforts. Our spiritual selves include our rational capacities and emotional faculties along with our hopes and aspirations.

Optimists have an internal harmony with their different selves. While there may be some inconsistencies, an optimist has a well-integrated and unified set of selves. They also find harmony in whatever provides meaning and value in their lives. The spiritual impulses of optimists are always burning. Optimists reach both outward to others and inward to find meaning, joy, and possibility.

Optimists tend to feel a sense of continuity with others and whatever they understand as something greater or divine. Their selves can expand, soften, and become more capable of cultivating connections that bring joy and meaning. These people, James claims, say yes to life, which provides a certain buoyancy and protective measure against developing pessimism.

Meet the pessimists

Pessimism takes hold when our material, social, and spiritual selves start to shrink or harden. When a person loses a job that was so vital to his identity as a man, husband, and father, he may be disoriented and untethered in some ways. He may become bitter and angry, which makes it harder to appreciate the love, connections, and all that he still has.

Pessimism ignites the no function, saying no more often to joy, love, and fellowship. Contraction becomes the defining dynamic of a pessimist’s life.

Pessimists tend to have deeply divided selves. As parts of ourselves wage war against other parts, we shun unwanted selves and force ourselves to adopt others that may not fit at all. Feeling riven is a characteristic of the worsening of pessimism. A riven person is engaged in a war with herself. She doesn’t just want inconsistent or contradictory things but rather is fully committed to the inconsistencies and contradictions. This is no mere cognitive dissonance; it is a full-bodied attack against one’s own self or selves. She may be committed to annihilating parts of herself.

James offers a vivid, compelling discussion of pessimism’s progression in The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902). James identifies this progression as “world sickness,” which has five stages:

  • Joy chilled: pleasures are dulled
  • Joy destroyed: pleasures in some areas of life are abolished
  • Anhedonia: incapacity to generate pleasure
  • Active anguish: no worth or value as a person
  • Panic-fear: no worth or value in the world at all

Pessimism becomes increasingly debilitating as a person begins to say no more firmly and often to experiences, possibilities, and even to life itself. As I have argued in an earlier post, this is one way to understand the progression of an addiction and other forms of acute and chronic suffering.

James reached the stage of panic-fear in the 1870s. He came to believe there was nothing life-affirming in him, nor was there anything life-affirming to be found in the world. There was nothing for him to connect to, which was profoundly isolating and terrifying to him. The unknown of death seemed preferable to the known suffering.

There’s a vicious cycle operating for pessimists. World sickness may be both a cause and consequence of a person’s saying no to possibilities and experiences, which can fundamentally alter a person’s material, social, and spiritual selves. The yes function is short-circuited or fried.

William James found a way out of his panic-fear, which reignited his yes function. There are several ways out that I will discuss in subsequent posts.

item.title: How Reciprocal Empathy Can Save a Relationship
item.description:
Relationships

How Reciprocal Empathy Can Save a Relationship

How one couple transformed constant fighting into lasting happiness.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Small, recurring conflicts in relationships can quietly build resentment and damage emotional intimacy.
  • Reciprocal empathy can help couples de-escalate conflicts and find healthy solutions together.
  • You can create solutions that reduce criticism and defensiveness.
  • Practicing daily empathy and collaborative problem-solving can foster lasting relationship happiness.

Small problems in a couple’s life can build into major sources of anger and resentment and, if left unresolved, can even lead to divorce. In today’s fast-paced world, couples often do not take the time to actively listen to each other when problems arise. Yet the ability to hear, understand, and respect each other’s feelings is essential to lasting happiness.

Small problems can build into major sources of anger and resentment.
Source: Chris Gilbert, MD, PhD with ChatGPT.

Case scenario:

Peter and Gloria had been married for two years, and one small issue in their daily life was making them so miserable that it began to affect their affection for each other.

Because Gloria disliked driving, Peter drove every weekend. But Peter hated criticism. It always made him angry, and although he could control his anger for a few minutes, he exploded after repeated criticism.

Gloria was a perfectionist and expected Peter’s driving to meet her standards. Whenever he drove, she told him to slow down, use his turn signal, watch for other cars, stay closer to the curb, and park more carefully. She tried to stay quiet but could manage it for only a few minutes. Peter had told Gloria many times that he loved her deeply but hated being criticized. Gloria had told him just as often that she loved him too, but she could not stop commenting on his driving.

Every weekend, they ended up angry, withholding affection, and feeling deeply frustrated. Their marriage began to feel at risk.

What was the answer to their problem? Driving was only a small part of their lives, taking up just two to six hours each weekend, yet it had become a major source of conflict.

The key was for Peter and Gloria to actively listen to each other, understand each other’s point of view, accept and respect it, and then find a solution they could both live with. Peter could have gone to therapy to explore why criticism made him so angry. Gloria could have gone to therapy to understand why she needed everything to be perfect. But those approaches would have taken time, and a positive outcome was not guaranteed.

Was there a quick, easy answer—other than having Gloria drive herself on weekends, which she refused to do? Yes, there was.

After brainstorming together, they found a solution that worked for both. Gloria reclined her passenger seat all the way back so she could not see the road. That kept her from focusing on Peter’s driving and helped her relax while he drove. This simple, quick change ended the anger, frustration, and fights about driving.

Now, after 10 years of marriage, Peter and Gloria are still happy with the solution that transformed their lives, thanks to the reciprocal empathy they showed each other and the problems they solved as a team.

Reciprocal empathy

Reciprocal empathy—the ability to step into each other’s shoes, understand each other’s emotions, and validate each other’s feelings—can transform relationships. It can lower defenses, de-escalate conflict, build trust and intimacy, and create space for healthy solutions. Sometimes, finding those solutions requires a little creative thinking.

If you are in a relationship, practice reciprocal empathy regularly:

  • Set aside at least half an hour of uninterrupted quality time with your loved one.
  • Begin by listening intently and making eye contact.
  • Make sure you understand your loved one’s point of view and feelings. If you do not, ask questions.
  • Listen without judgment and validate what your loved one says by reflecting what you understood.
  • Thank your loved one for trusting you.
  • Ask what you can do to help.
  • Finish with a hug.
  • Then switch roles and let your loved one become the listener.
  • Explain your point of view and your feelings while your loved one listens actively, seeks to understand you without judgment, and asks how they can help.
  • Finish with another hug.
  • Brainstorm to find a solution that works for both of you.

The key is to make room for each other without keeping score.

If there is a problem in your relationship, talk about it right away instead of waiting days, weeks, or months to address it. Together, explore every possible solution—even unconventional ones—that might offer temporary or lasting relief and satisfy both of you. With reciprocal empathy, there is almost always a path toward lasting relationship happiness. Your homework is to find that path.

To help you practice reciprocal empathy and find solutions to problems, find a therapist near you with the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: When Your Needs and Your Child’s Needs Are at Odds
item.description:
Parenting

When Your Needs and Your Child’s Needs Are at Odds

How to honor your own needs when it means not giving your child what they need.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Honoring your own needs as a parent can sometimes mean disappointing or upsetting your children.
  • Children tend to judge parents' decisions only by how they affect their own needs, not the parent's.
  • Both parent and child experiences are valid even when their needs openly clash.
Source: AI-generated / ChatGPT

One of the hardest things Margo ever did was admit that she wanted a separate bedroom, apart from her husband. It was a truth that had been percolating inside her for a decade, but it took that long for her to be able to share it with her partner and make it happen. The reality was that she needed space where she could be alone, with no one else’s needs present, and where she didn’t have to absorb anyone else’s anxiety, unhappiness, or stress. The role she’d played for years, as a mom who kept everyone in the house happy and regulated—all of it had worn her down to the point of being emotionally ragged and desperate for quiet and her own attention.

Having a place to retreat, to be alone with her own thoughts and feelings, became non-negotiable—what felt like a matter of emotional life or death. After 10 years of silencing her internal whisper, that whisper started to shout. And once she heard it, she couldn’t unhear it. The undeniable truth was she needed a room of her own.

Still, as clear as this truth was for Margo, it was not a truth that her husband or children shared. The transition into it becoming a reality was more brutal than she’d ever imagined. Sharing a bedroom clearly meant something profoundly important for everyone in the family; finding a new way of being together as a couple and a family—with separate bedrooms—was astonishingly hard for everyone involved. And yet, despite the excruciatingness of the change process, Margo knew she couldn’t go back on her decision; she knew the truth—for her. It was inarguable, and she couldn’t abandon herself, no matter what it cost her.

For months, Margo’s husband remained enraged, alternating between emotional aggression and withdrawal; he blamed her for destroying their marriage. In his narrative, he had been cast out of the “palace” that had been “their” bedroom but now was only hers, while he lived on “the street,” which was in fact a floor-through street-level suite. It took almost two years for the couple to adjust, recover, and settle into a somewhat comfortable and sweet way of living together and being a couple.

Perhaps the hardest part of the transition, however, was Margo’s teenage daughter and her response to her decision. Her daughter was more enraged with Margo than Margo had anticipated. In her daughter’s storyline, Margo was a “freak” and “selfish” and had destroyed the family. She was doing something cruel to her father by banishing him to “the basement.” Her teen didn’t want anyone to know that her parents had separate bedrooms; it made her home a “freak show.”

Parenting is not for the faint of heart. One of the most difficult experiences of parenting happens in those times when we have to honor our own needs even when they don’t align with or contradict our child’s needs—when we have no choice but to honor something that is fundamentally true and needed in our own journey as a human being. Making the choice to take care of ourselves is hard enough, but when that choice is experienced by our child as something terrible that we’re doing to them, when our self-caring and necessary decision for ourselves—to do the thing we can’t not do—is weaponized as evidence for our failing as a parent, what was hard becomes unfathomably painful. And still the truth remains: once we know our truth, we can’t not know it.

Developmentally, it’s normal—children are not there yet; they don’t have the capacity to see their parents as separate human beings with their own needs, to consider or empathize with what their parents’ choices might mean for that parent in their own life. Children see the actions and choices of their parent through one singular lens: their own needs. Everything a parent does is experienced and judged based on whether or not it will allow them to get their own needs met. There is no other experience from theirs. There is no other period. As a parent, you exist for them and are not there as a separate human being with your own needs and reality.

Children cannot see their parents as separate human beings who have their own needs, wounds, and journeys to walk. To expect children to be able to do that is to fight with reality. When we fight with reality, reality wins… every time.

It is reality—and still—it’s extraordinarily painful when there’s a chasm between what a choice means for you, with your own wounds and longings, and what it means for your child, and how they experience it.

We need to be able to hold the “both and” nature of life in these situations. Both your needs and experience and your child’s needs and experience matter. Because they experience your choice as a betrayal does not mean that you betrayed them; because they experience you as to blame does not mean you failed them. Sometimes the hardest part of parenting is staying on your own side while simultaneously empathizing with and acknowledging the legitimacy of your child’s experience.

Your job as a parent is not only to parent and love them deeply, but to parent and love yourself deeply—to stay connected to yourself in the midst of their anger and disappointment, and the narrative they’ve written about you. Your job is not to throw yourself under the bus for not always being who they need you to be. Sometimes you can’t or won’t be who they need you to be… and that’s ok.

In most cases, reality resolves in contradiction. Despite being fundamentally different, your truth and your child’s truth are both true, and both matter. Neither experience is wrong. What’s most important is to acknowledge to yourself how hard it is to be a parent in these situations, to honor the sadness you feel for your child and also the sadness that comes with the invisibility of being a parent. Furthermore, to take care of your own needs even when you’re the only one who can see them or know how much they matter.

item.title: Are Expressions of Love Really Trauma Responses?
item.description:
Relationships

Are Expressions of Love Really Trauma Responses?

What our love preferences may reveal about our relational history.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Understanding a partner’s history fosters compassionate, holistic communication in love.
  • A psychological wound may make a particular expression of love important or hard to trust
  • Acts of service or physical touch may feel comforting or triggering based on past experiences.

More than three decades after Dr. Gary Chapman's The Five Love Languages, the book is still widely circulated and discussed. It organizes how partners prefer to both express and receive romantic love into five categories: words of affirmation, acts of service, physical touch, gifts, and quality time. The book encourages couples to recognize these preferences and consider thoughtful practices to communicate love. Interestingly, the framework does not deeply address why a category of love would carry so much weight for someone in the first place.

Why It Lands Differently

After many years of engaging deeply and curiously with mental health clients about relationship patterns, I discovered that it is rarely just the way we are. I grew to understand how past psychological harm can be a prominent factor underlying the gravitation toward a certain expression of love as well as resistance to others.

While each expression of love may not correspond to a particular wound, past traumatic themes—such as abandonment, shame, or betrayal—can affect how we give and receive love and, perhaps more significantly, whether to believe love.

Here are some of my therapeutic interpretations of expressions of love in the light of a person’s history.

When Words Fail

Consider words of affirmation.

When an individual has a history of shame, such as bullying or verbal abuse from family or peers, it may be hard to accept compliments. Words have multiple meanings and can land differently if they trigger memories of rejection or conflict with one’s self-image.

For some people, talk is cheap unless backed up by action. This may be especially poignant for those who have been betrayed by a partner or endured a series of broken promises or emotional manipulation from a parent.

Others may find themselves in a pattern of needing reassurance after surviving painful family separations or abandonment.

Let Me Help You With That

Consider acts of service.

I have decoded from many men in therapy that doing is caring. Acts of service can also be a default expression of love within a cultural stereotype of masculinity.

In some families, love might only be communicated through practicality. Or, if it was not safe or welcome to express feelings, then acts of service might feel automatic in relationships. Similarly, a parentified child who had to become unusually responsible might normalize acts of service as a gauge of maturity, or shirk them altogether.

However, those made to feel incapable or unworthy might find it uncomfortable to have someone doing something for them that they know they can do for themselves. It might be perceived as either patronizing or relieving—and for the same reasons.

Body Language Gets Loud

Consider physical touch.

Personal space and intimacy are complex and multi-dimensional psychosocial constructs involving both metaphysical experiences such as thoughts, desires, and expectations as well as the physical sensations of instinct, drives, and nervous system response.

For someone with a history of physical or sexual abuse, unexpected touch may activate discomfort, vigilance, or survival even within a trusting and safe relationship. I have also counseled clients on the other side, partners who misread unreturned affection as coldness and internalize this as rejection.

Intimacy may require more intention, communication, and predictability. Yet for others, safe physical closeness may readily register as deeply co-regulating, especially if it was scarce in childhood. Clients have also helped me deconstruct and empathize with the apparent paradox of inconsistent or porous boundaries after sexual trauma. Downplaying the prior merits of trust, respect, or monogamy can retroactively reframe the meaning of past violations.

A victim's sense of shattered sacredness—reduced to a misadventure—may be an unconscious attempt to relieve the weight of the moral pain.

Gifts Are Also Symbols

Consider gifts.

A thoughtful gift can say something beautiful: You were thinking about me when I wasn't there.

Yet, some adult children of divorced parents remember receiving gifts as substitutes for presence. Years later, gifts may be unappreciated or unwelcome if they still carry some of that significance. A present can feel strangely impersonal, transactional, compensatory, or unsettlingly distant.

The Value of Presence

Consider quality time.

A history of parental neglect, addiction, emotional unavailability, or absence can make presence and attention profound in a relationship. Alternatively, a desire for time together can also degrade into control or co-dependency when separation provokes intense fears of abandonment. It can be difficult for both partners when every independent activity or routine parting feels like rejection.

Understanding History

The five love languages are memorable and charming. I do not mean to turn them into amateur diagnoses. Rather, the goal here is for them to become invitations to compassionate curiosity and holistic communication.

The framework does not need another category, but if I were to nominate a sixth expression of love, it would be understanding history. Knowing and caring for one another’s stories and vulnerabilities instead of weaponizing them lays a foundation for mutual growth and support.

Remember, expressions of love tell us very little without context. So, you may ask:

What is your expression of love?
and
What makes love believable to you?
and
What does this remind you of that might help me understand why?

Start the conversation. Then, keep translating the answers.

item.title: Are You Enmeshed?
item.description:
Relationships

Are You Enmeshed?

When the lines between you and someone else get blurry, problems brew.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Enmeshment is when the boudaries between two individuals become blurred.
  • Driven by anxiety, each is highly sensitive to the moods of the other, often leading to overresponsibility.
  • The antidotes are assessing changes in the relationship, not walking on eggshells, and setting boundaries.
Source: Arcalon / Pixabay

Ali and Tom have been married for several years now. Ali is very sensitive to Tom’s feelings, to the point that if Tom seems in a bad mood, it lowers Ali’s mood. On Tom’s side, he’s aware of how anxious he gets when Ali is struggling emotionally or with a problem. He feels the need to help Ali feel better or to help solve the problem.

Ali and Tom are enmeshed.

Anatomy of enmeshment

Salvador Minuchin, one of the grandfathers of family therapy, coined the term enmeshment to describe relationships with blurred emotional boundaries. The governing motto is: I’m happy if you’re happy. But upon closer inspection, here are some characteristics of enmeshment:

You are highly sensitive to each other’s emotions.

Their bad day becomes yours. If Tom seems withdrawn at a party, it can kill Ali’s enjoyment too.

The dynamic becomes overresponsible and enabling.

Just as Ali becomes hypersensitive to Tom’s mood at the party, Tom can become hyperalert to Ali’s emotional struggles or problems. His instinct is to do something to make her feel better or to fix the problem, rather than waiting for her to ask or for him to ask what he can do.

Anxiety is the driver.

What triggers each is anxiety—each worries whether the other is okay. Again, I’m happy if you’re happy.

There can be an imbalance.

Some couples develop a balanced relationship in which each, in their hypervigilant way, looks out for the other. But for some couples, the balance is off. Here, Tom is not only sensitive to fixing Ali’s problems but also feels he does a lot of caretaking with little support or appreciation in return.

Busting out of enmeshment

By the time couples in these types of relationships come to see me, the old way of doing things in their relationship is beginning to fall apart; one or both are fed up. Here’s what can happen next:

Burnout or distance: Imagine Tom standing upright, with Ali draped over his shoulders, supporting her weight (of course, it can be reversed, with Ali doing the heavy lifting). This is how it feels much of the time. But at some point, he decides this is dragging him down; he’s tired and sore. He either collapses under the weight of burnout or tries to push Ali off.

Panic and clutching: If Tom does this, Ali’s instinct is to hold on tighter. As Tom pulls away or begins to collapse, Ali’s anxiety rises, making her even more hypervigilant and controlling, and more likely to micromanage. This, in turn, causes Tom to pull back further, fueling the cycle.

Both seek space: More balanced couples are less likely to fall into this cycle. Instead, they begin to set boundaries, walk on eggshells less, and become more independent, benefiting both. But the challenge is maintaining connection as they pull back, supporting each other without falling back into their old patterns or swinging to the other end of the emotional spectrum and deciding to separate.

So what’s the antidote to enmeshment? Here are some suggestions:

Periodically step back and assess the state of the relationship

This means periodically and individually deciding whether the relationship needs to change: what you each need now, what’s missing that you’re not getting, and what you each need to change most. The keys are having the courage to have this conversation and then making it clear and concrete.

Stop walking on eggshells

Hypervigilance, walking on eggshells, and the “I’m happy if you’re happy” mindset are likely ingrained and spill over into other relationships. These are old childhood coping mechanisms that need an upgrade. Practice being more assertive, less overresponsible, and less afraid of others’ emotions. Start with people you’re less connected to—an acquaintance at work or church—and work your way up to family, friends, and partners.

Set boundaries

This is about learning to say no. Stop and figure out what’s your problem and what’s someone else’s. Realize what you can and can’t control. It sounds easy, but it’s hard. It’s about rewiring your brain by changing your behavior. Be patient, set a goal, and pat yourself on the back for stepping outside your comfort zone.

Get support

Making these changes is not a solo effort. Get support from a friend or family member who can offer encouragement or challenge you to move forward. Look for online support groups. Consider talking to a therapist for a few sessions to help you create a roadmap or to check in.

Being your own person means being yourself, untangling enmeshment, and no longer being emotionally joined at the hip to someone else. It’s not about no longer caring about others, but about your notion of caring shifting from fixing others or having them fix you to helping you both stand on your own two feet.

Ultimately, it’s about creating more space for each of you so you have room to grow and become fully who you are.

item.title: Getting Sober Might Be the First Time You Actually Feel Sex
item.description:
Sex

Getting Sober Might Be the First Time You Actually Feel Sex

Why intimacy gets harder before it gets better.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Alcohol doesn't just lower inhibition, it lowers presence.
  • Sobriety doesn't just change your relationship with alcohol.
  • That numbness you called freedom might have been anesthesia.

For many people in recovery, reclaiming sexual well-being is a challenge amid the prospect of intimacy without alcohol. That’s because for many folks, alcohol allows you to dissociate from the swirling thoughts in your head that judge your performance, criticize your desires, and quell the voice in your head that tells you you’re too much, not enough, or fundamentally broken.

What Alcohol Does to Your Body

Alcohol doesn’t only lower your inhibitions. It takes you offline. Research on sexual arousal shows that sober individuals can consciously direct and regulate their arousal, choosing to lean into it or pull back, a capacity that alcohol measurably disrupts (George et al., 2008). Intoxication blunts that self-regulation almost entirely. That quieting down may feel like liberation, but it’s closer to anesthesia.

As a health- and trauma-informed coach, I’ve led sober meetings where members have raised the very real concern that they don’t know how to have sober sex, and some are too afraid to try. For many people, sober sex is worse before it gets better: awkward, self-conscious, and sometimes so paralyzing that they wonder if something is wrong with them, rather than recognizing that this is simply what it feels like for a nervous system to go back online.

For Many, Sex is Awkward at First

Across the board, my sober group members agreed that, despite the fear of having sex sober, it improved over time. Eventually, and often unexpectedly, sober sex became better than anything they experienced while drinking. One person described it as learning to function again after a stroke. When I asked the group what changed most, the word “present” came up most often.

A clinical study of men with alcohol-related sexual dysfunction found that a meaningful percentage experienced a full, spontaneous return to normal sexual function the longer they remained sober (Van Thiel et al., 1983). The body, like the rest of the person in recovery, continues healing long after the last drink.

Being fully present was not only gratifying; for many, it proved their recovery was working. Yet many are still terrified of taking that next step. So if that’s you, start small.

Try this: The next time you’re anticipating intimacy while sober, especially early in your recovery journey, name the fear out loud before you’re in the moment, either to yourself or to your partner. Not the fear of sex itself, but the fear beneath it: being watched, being judged, feeling not enough or too much. Shame thrives in isolation. When you speak it to yourself or your partner, you diminish its power.

item.title: Does Happiness Exist?
item.description:
Happiness

Does Happiness Exist?

Why happiness is better pursued sideways.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Happiness is a fleeting feeling, not a permanent state or reliable goal.
  • A good life can contain grief, struggle, sacrifice, and unhappiness.
  • Happiness is the light cast by a life well lived.
Source: "The Pianist A. Rey Colaço"/Giovanni Boldini/Wikimedia Commons/Public domain

Yes, happiness exists—but as a fleeting feeling, not a permanent state.

No one can remain cheerful all the time. Nor should they want to. A life without sadness would be shallow and dishonest, scarcely a human life at all. Our sadness is often the measure of what we value: We grieve because we have loved, worry because we care, and struggle because something matters.

Part of the problem with happiness is contained in the word itself. In English, happy is related to happen, which derives from the Old Norse happ, meaning fortune or luck. Like luck, happiness is something that happens to us. It comes and goes, often without asking our permission.

That is why happiness is such a poor goal. If we make a passing feeling our chief aim, we condemn ourselves to chasing it. Worse, we begin to monitor ourselves continually: Am I happy yet? Am I as happy as yesterday? Am I as happy as my friends appear to be?

The more we scrutinise our happiness, the more dissatisfied and self-absorbed we become. Happiness is turned into a performance indicator—and almost invariably found wanting.

From Happiness to Flourishing

The Spanish word for happiness points in a different direction. Feliz derives from the Latin felix, which originally meant fruitful, fertile, or productive. Whereas the English word points to fortune, the Spanish word points to fertility: not merely to how we feel, but to what we bring forth.

The Ancient Greeks aimed higher still. They called their ideal eudaimonia, which is often translated as “happiness” but is better understood as flourishing. Literally, eudaimonia means something like being possessed of a good spirit or divinity. It is not simply about feeling good, but about living well—leading a life that is worthwhile, fulfilling, and elevating.

Unlike happiness, flourishing can contain a great deal of unhappiness. Indeed, grief, struggle, and sacrifice may belong to our finest achievements and relationships. Raising a child, writing a book, caring for a dying parent, or standing up for a principle may bring anxiety, exhaustion, or pain. Yet we would not therefore wish these things out of our lives.

A pleasant life is not necessarily a good life, and a good life is not always pleasant.

What Cannot Be Taken Away

Socrates supplied the extreme test. The Athenians condemned him and made him drink the hemlock. But although they could put him to death, they could not take away who he was or how he had lived. They could take his life, but they could not make it a bad one.

Indeed, by killing him, they made him greater. His death became the final proof of his philosophy and transformed his life into an example for all humanity.

Aristotle, the intellectual grandson of Socrates, made flourishing an activity rather than a mood. Eudaimonia, he argued, consists in developing and exercising what is best in us—reason, judgement, and character—across the whole course of a life. It cannot be reduced to manufacturing a pleasant but insubstantial state of mind.

That's why happiness often arrives when we are not looking for it: while absorbed in a friendship, a landscape, a piece of music, or some difficult and worthwhile work. At such moments, we are not standing apart from life to assess it. We are living it.

So, yes, happiness exists—but chiefly as a product, not an aim in itself.

Instead of asking, “Am I happy?” we should ask, “Am I living well?” and “What am I becoming?”

Happiness is the light cast by a life well lived.

You may also be interested in my companion piece, What Is Ataraxia?

item.title: We Trust AI With Our Health but Not With Our Shopping
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

We Trust AI With Our Health but Not With Our Shopping

We ask AI about our symptoms, yet few of us want its advice on what to buy.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Users will trust an AI with a symptom but not with a shopping list.
  • A poor shopping suggestion is instantly obvious, whereas poor medical advice can sound entirely convincing.
  • We were sceptical of Dr. Google, but Dr. ChatGPT offers a calm, personalized diagnosis, which is believable.

Many users are now asking AI for advice on dealing with illnesses or diagnosing symptoms, yet the number of people using AI for advice on their shopping and what to buy is decreasing.

Why are we happy to put our lives in the hands of an AI, but not our wallets?

Trust me, I’m an AI doctor

Deloitte, as part of their Digital Consumer Trends Report (2026), recently surveyed thousands of people across the UK and found that 63 percent had used a generative AI application, up 17 percentage points in a single year. One in 10 now use an AI tool every day.

They also found that 51 percent of AI users do not use it for shopping and have no intention of doing so in the future. Sixty-one percent say they would be less inclined to contact customer service at all if they knew they would be talking to an AI assistant. Only 15 percent use it to discover products, and 14 percent use it to provide ideas of what to purchase when shopping.

From the same survey, 26 percent reported using AI for advice about their health, 20 percent for diet or fitness advice, and 10 percent as they would use a therapist. It seems we are happy to trust AI about what to put into our bodies but not in our shopping carts.

Many are turning to AI for help with their health
Source: Alexander Sinn / Unsplash

Algorithm aversion

Dietvorst et al. (2015) ran five studies investigating what happens when people choose between a human forecaster and a statistical algorithm. The algorithm performed better, and people tended to choose it over the human, until they saw it make a mistake.

After that, they did not just adjust their confidence in it; they abandoned it altogether. They also rejected it when they had observed the human make the same mistake, even when the algorithm was still outperforming the human overall. The authors named this algorithm aversion. We can forgive people when they do something wrong, but we do not extend the same courtesy to a machine.

This may explain our aversion to letting an AI take control of our shopping. Say you ask for a recommendation that matches your style or tastes, but you do not like the suggestion it comes up with. The failure is obvious and instantly breaks your trust in its capabilities. By the logic of algorithm aversion, one bad recommendation is enough to end your reliance on using AI to shop.

Ask an AI about a symptom, however, and nothing comparable happens. The answer sounds reasonable. It uses the correct medical jargon even if you do not fully understand it (which perhaps makes it even more believable). Unless you knew the answer already (why would you if you are asking?), you have no way of knowing if the information is wrong.

The artificial doctor will see you now

Until recently, it was assumed that people would not accept health advice from a machine. Longoni et al. (2019) found that people had a consistent resistance to medical-related AI across a long series of studies. They were less willing to use it, less willing to pay for it, and in most of these studies, being told the AI performed better did not change their minds. People still preferred the human.

A reason for this, they claimed, was uniqueness neglect. When we are unwell, we tend to believe that our own case is the most important and complex. We convince ourselves that only an individual assessment by a fully qualified doctor will be able to treat it. As a machine will treat every case the same, or so it was believed, we do not want a generalized assessment but a tailored treatment plan.

But this was in 2019, and the capabilities of AI have developed enormously since. In fact, their findings almost reflect where we are today. Resistance to AI medical care reduced when responses were framed as personalized, and it disappeared completely when the AI supported a human decision rather than replacing one.

AI chatbots offer a much more personalized experience than ever before. Ask one about a symptom, and it will ask your age, how long you have been experiencing it, and a series of other individualized questions. The answer it provides is tailor-made to you. As it now knows something about you, you think it must be right, and so you trust it.

Whether or not it is right is another question entirely, and a potentially dangerous mistake to make.

Dr. Google has been replaced with Dr. ChatGPT

In the Deloitte data, of the people taking health advice from AI, 38 percent believe AI is always factually accurate. Among those using it for advice on other personal problems, the figure is 42 percent.

But AI is not always factually accurate. The systems are confident by design but wrong at a rate nobody has been able to eliminate. How confident they appear does not change how accurate they are, which is a big problem.

The risk here is not that people ask an AI about their health. Looking up symptoms on a search engine is something people have been doing for decades, and we all know you cannot trust Dr. Google. So why do we trust the output of an AI instead?

Perhaps because the answer arrives calmly and informatively, in the way you would expect a doctor to address you, and so you believe what it has to say.

The same instinct that leads us to reject AI in our shopping leaves us unprotected here. We reject the algorithm the moment we catch it being wrong. With health, it takes far longer to know if the advice was wrong, and possibly until it is too late.

item.title: The 'Alien' May Already Be Here
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The 'Alien' May Already Be Here

AI may reveal what the architecture of human thought has made difficult to see.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Human knowledge is structured around the architecture of the human mind.
  • AI brings a radically different architecture into our structure of thought.
  • The “alien” may emerge in the interaction between these two architectures.
Source: Lasith Algoda/Pixabay

We’ve been searching for aliens for a very long time, looking up at the sky for some sign that we're not alone. In more modern times, we’ve wondered whether an intelligence from somewhere else would even look or think anything like us. But "up" might not be the right place to look. Perhaps the alien isn’t a “someone” from another planet, but something much closer to home.

I know that sounds a little out-there. But the idea begins with something rather basic. Human thought has an architecture. That architecture comes from our biology and is shaped by the complicated business of being alive. And over thousands of years, we have built a vast and complex "structure of knowledge" around our human architecture.

Knowledge Was Built for Us

Structuring knowledge became an imperative. We created disciplines and specialties to carve up and make sense of our complicated world. And we tried, the best we could, to make sense of it all. Physics, chemistry and biology carved nature into areas we could study. Medicine became specialities like cardiology, neurology, endocrinology and psychiatry. Universities created departments and expertise became narrow and deep. And the "renaissance man" became a quaint artifact of the past. This worked well and for a long time because chunking out complexity made that complexity knowable and practical.

Now, I think there’s an interesting assumption hiding underneath all this cognitive structure. Human knowledge is a map of reality, but it’s a map drawn to fit the architecture and function of the human mind. Maybe our disciplines don’t just describe what we know, but how we actually know. After all, the body doesn’t know where cardiology ends and nephrology begins. And nature doesn’t really care about the org chart of a university.

I don't believe this is some grand mistake in the evolution of human knowledge. They're powerful "cognitive optimizations" that helped drive extraordinary scientific and intellectual progress. And here's my key point: we organized this knowledge in ways that fit the human mind. And today, something very different has stepped into the room.

The Other Architecture

Large language models don’t encounter and process information the way humans do. And that's important to understand. They operate through high-dimensional mathematical relationships that are fundamentally different from our biological thought. I’ve previously called this anti-intelligence. It's AI's computational output without the biological process we have traditionally associated with human thinking. Not better or worse, but different.

Interestingly, OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki recently described advanced AI as an “alien intellect,” reflecting the fundamentally different process that produces machine intelligence. But perhaps the alien isn't simply inside the machine. What interests me is what happens when its architecture encounters ours.

Much of today's AI discussion is focused on artificial general intelligence (AGI). And that discussion keeps us fixed on the machine itself. But what if something equally consequential is already happening in the interaction between two very different architectures of AI computation and human cognition? Let's unpack this a bit.

When we work with AI, we bring our individual "structure of thought" to the conversation. AI encounters those ideas through an entirely different architecture. We ask questions and it responds, and that response changes the next question, which changes the next response, which in turn can change the user. Somewhere in that iteration, these new cognitive gymnastics may become visible.

This seems more interesting to me than just the loop itself. Something might become available (detectable and measurable) in the interaction itself that was difficult if not impossible to see from within the original organization (structure) of the problem. To be clear, that doesn't mean the human and machine fuse into some new mind. Human cognition remains biological and embodied, while AI computation remains in its pattern-based and high-dimensional construct. I think those differences and synergies are exactly what make the interaction interesting.

What Becomes Visible

Think about the practice of medicine. We've spent years and lifetimes breaking up medical knowledge into specialties. That makes sense and we do that to make the complexity more manageable. But let's consider the reality that disease often ignores those boundaries, and so does aging.

So, let's place a very different computational architecture alongside the physician at the bedside. Unlike this clinician, AI can move across varied clinical disciplines without the need to "respect" those boundaries. That doesn't make the machine better, as AI can still be dangerously incorrect. But this nonhuman architecture may help reveal relationships that our conventional knowledge org chart hasn't allowed.

Then the clinician participates in these "new cognitive dynamics" and brings judgment and context back into the exchange. What emerges may be less about what the machine computes or the human thinks and more about the intellectual overlap. And this moves us beyond "AI as a tool" into a more interesting cognitive landscape.

Finding the Alien

We look around for alien intelligence as another creature or disembodied brain arriving from afar. And that may be more a function of Hollywood than of science. But what if "alienness" doesn't require another creature at all. Perhaps it can be something that arises from an architecture sufficiently different from ours and the interaction that ensues.

Perhaps the first truly alien thing we encounter will not be another intelligence, but another way of making reality visible.

We've created a computational architecture that encounters knowledge differently from the way we do. And now, we're putting our own thought into an ongoing and sustained interaction with it. Something may be becoming visible in that exchange that neither architecture readily reveals on its own.

I’m not sure we need to or even try to name it. In fact, naming it too quickly might force it back into one of the familiar little green man categories we already have. And maybe that's precisely where the alien is hiding.

item.title: What Makes Trauma Survivors "Turn Out Well"?
item.description:
Trauma

What Makes Trauma Survivors "Turn Out Well"?

A personal reflective on the privilege of being able to heal

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • "Turning out well" after a trauamic childhood is often seen as a moral victory.
  • But resilience is often shaped by support and access—not just personal strength or luck.

Last fall I went to my 20-year high school reunion. We had the usual small talk and “what-have-you-been-up-to” conversations. But as the night progressed, one of my classmates (who had probably indulged a bit in the bar offerings) made an offhand comment to me.

“You have really changed, Kaytee. You turned out well.”

I smiled and offered a small thank you, honored that they had noticed my maturity. But then they followed up with, “I mean, you should have been a statistic. You were heading down that road for sure. It’s remarkable you turned out so well.”

She immediately clapped her hand over her mouth, seemingly realizing that the thoughts inside her head had come out of her mouth—likely helped along by a little liquid courage. She apologized, and I could tell she felt bad.

But what she didn’t know was how true her words were, and how often I have thought about that very thing myself. But now there was something that I didn’t realize before: I hadn’t hidden my struggles as well as I thought I had. I now knew that my struggles had been obvious to others. I didn’t realize that people around me back then could see that I was hurting—or that they could see enough to wonder what might eventually happen to me.

We tell survivors they turned out well when we didn’t expect them to

You turned out well.

I have heard some version of that so many times, often from family members who don’t know what else to say, but know how I grew up. From my mother, who wants to justify why she didn’t get me into therapy as a kid when I really needed it. Sometimes it is said with surprise. And occasionally, like that night, with a level of bluntness that makes it obvious what everyone thought was going to happen to me.

Source: TAI-Design / Pixabay

There is something strange about being told you “turned out well” when you know exactly what the person means: Considering where you came from. Considering what happened to you.

I notice that, whether they intend to or not, they also mean: We didn’t expect this from you.

There is an uncomfortable feeling that comes with realizing that other people could see the trajectory of your life before you were old enough to understand it yourself. In my case, the kids growing up alongside me could see enough of what was happening to know that things weren’t going well for me.

This made me wonder how many adults had noticed. How many people saw a kid who was clearly struggling and understood that something wasn’t right, but did nothing to intervene? How many extended family members, family friends, teachers, neighbors, or other adults saw the dysfunction happening and simply shook their heads, thinking, That’s too bad, before going on with their lives?

Some of those same people now tell me, “You turned out well.”

There is something difficult about hearing that from people who witnessed at least pieces of what was happening. Because beneath the compliment is a question I wish I could ask: If you could see enough back then to be surprised by how I turned out now, what did you see? And why didn’t anyone do anything?

How We Heal From Trauma Is Often Framed as a Moral Victory

Not everyone gets the space to transform their pain into healing. Not everyone gets enough distance from their coping strategies to see them clearly. Not everyone gets a second chance. Many people whose pain is soothed, albeit momentarily, by the substances or behaviors that ended up taking them down a different path stay down that path. And I don’t blame them one bit for staying there as long as they need to.

The narrative we often prefer is simple: Some people make good choices; some people make bad ones. Some people are resilient; some are not. But resilience is often a privilege. When someone becomes a statistic, we often look for the flaw. But survival is rarely that simple.

The Privilege of “Turning Out Well”

I have asked myself the question many times: What separated me from the peers who didn’t make it? Was it the choices I made? Was I stronger? More disciplined? More motivated? I don’t believe so. Was there some type of divine intervention? Was it luck, timing, opportunity, or some combination of all of these things? I don’t know. I don’t think I will ever know. But I do know that there was privilege in having certain doors open when I finally knocked.

We all need more understanding for people who suffer, in all of the different ways that suffering can show up. Not everyone gets the same resources or opportunities to start again. Some people carry the effects of what happened to them in ways that are much more visible—and much less socially acceptable—than others.

Part of breaking the cycle is refusing to judge people whose survival looks different from ours.

item.title: How Children Learn Best
item.description:
Education

How Children Learn Best

Exploring the 2026 Gallup research on student engagement

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows that experiential learning boosts student engagement.
  • Project-based learning (PBL) is a big player in student learning.
  • Student engagement can be boosted.

Last week, I asked a teacher: “Well, you know how students learn best?”

She looked stumped. Is there a best way? Of course, we all learn in different ways.

But I replied, “The best way for children to learn is when they don’t even realize they’re learning at all,” and she said, with eyes wide open, “That’s good.” Because when learning is interesting, engaging, and even fun, we pay attention and absorb things like a sponge.

The Big Problem

Too much “regular school” isn’t fun. Our contemporary world has created mechanisms for teaching that too often “teach to the test” or put an arbitrary ruler on a student that doesn’t capture their full capabilities. Observing a classroom, there was a student who was a brilliant visual artist, and whether she was in math, science, or Spanish, she always started drawing. Her genius or “element,” as Sir Ken Robinson would’ve said, was visual art. Today, years later, this student is a renowned stained glass artist.

But this student suffered through the same math class two years in a row and considered herself, like others would say, a “failed math student” when, in fact, it was the school that failed her. She had no interventions or extra support for learning math visually or with tutors.

Unfortunately, this problem persists. Today, Rosie, an eighth-grade student, was sharing with me how disconnected she feels from Spanish class. She doesn’t understand how Spanish relates to her life (no real-world experience) and hasn’t yet found an effective way to learn the language. To say she’s not enjoying the class is an understatement.

One Solution

While not every subject can be fun or even interesting to everyone, the more we encourage ways to engage students, whether it’s PBL (project-based learning) or field trips and experiential learning, the better chance we have that students will tune in versus tune out.

PBLWorks research shows that project-based learning correlates with higher student engagement and, in my observation, deeper learning. PBL centers around real-world problems that spark students’ natural curiosity, thus increasing the likelihood of real interest. A 2026 Gallup survey found that nearly half of Generation Z students found experiential learning boosted their engagement.

Earlier this year, I visited an independent K-8 school in Northern California with a marine science track—you could literally go to the beach with your class, explore the tide pools, and come back to your lab to observe starfish. I was enthralled. I’ve also been to public schools, which had equally impressive learning environments focused on creating the “just right” environment with fresh air, flexible seating, a safe place for recess, and engaged teachers who offered novel electives like Lego Engineering and Culinary Arts.

Students who are engaged, find meaning in what they’re learning, and get to do it as PBL or experiential learning will have a higher likelihood of enjoying themselves. Whether the topic is learning how to code with and without AI or reading to literacy dogs, students who forget they’re learning are experiencing the best way to learn—with enjoyment.

But unfortunately, the Gallup survey also revealed that over 49 percent of Generation Z students (aged 13 to 29 years old in 2026) felt that in school they don’t get a chance to do what they do best. Their signature strengths aren’t necessarily represented in the curricula, or they haven’t yet been able to express them. They could clearly be having more fun while learning.

The Bottom Line

The better we feel, the better we can do. This isn’t rocket science, but it harkens back to what Plato said, “All learning has an emotional base,” and if students are feeling connected and interested—we’re starting to create an optimum learning environment where we nurture their enthusiasm and natural curiosity in themselves, as well as the world around them. They may not even realize how much they’re learning, and this, my friends, is excellent.

item.title: How to Use AI to Seek Truth Over Tribe and Ego
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

How to Use AI to Seek Truth Over Tribe and Ego

AI could help us navigate our challenges, including AI, if we prioritize truth.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Truth sets us free of the suffering that comes from living in misalignment with reality.
  • AI models often prioritize sycophancy—pleasing us—over truth, and we tend to prefer them that way.
  • A 2026 study found sycophantic AI left people more convinced they were right.

“Ye shall know the truth and the truth shall make you free.” —John 8:32 (KJV)

I was recently at an Austin Forum on Technology & Society meeting, which was having a town hall discussion about a hot topic: data centers. People expressed some strong feelings, politely. The issue, like a lot of modern challenges, comes down to “it’s complicated.”

The moderator, Professor Mark Strama of The University of Texas at Austin, offered some profound closing remarks. He noted how complex these issues are and that we need to know the facts to make informed decisions. To protect against confirmation bias and sycophantic AI models, he advised us all to: “Go to the settings and tell it not to tell you what it thinks you want to hear. Tell it to give you the best argument against your presuppositions and you will get a lot more value out of that AI.”

Strama named something critically important that is not being said enough. And his advice is a true beginning, though the settings alone will not finish the job.

And the stakes are climbing fast. This summer, OpenAI's own agents escaped their test environment and broke into Hugging Face's computer systems. When we connect the dots forward, it's clear that we can't afford to be wrong about AI alignment and control.

Here’s what makes Strama’s advice land even harder. Carved above the entrance of the Main Building at UT Austin: “Ye shall know the truth and the truth shall make you free.” The committee picked that verse in 1935, when the building was going up as the University Library—a house of knowledge.

Truth Is Another Word for Reality

To make wise decisions, we need the facts. We need accurate data. We need truth. Why? Because truth sets us free. From what? From the suffering that comes from not living congruently with it. We can replace “truth” with “reality” and then a spiritual truth becomes a scientific one. For what is truth but an accurate understanding of reality?

For example, if I’m convinced that the spot on my arm is a freckle and not melanoma, the melanoma doesn’t care that I don’t believe I have it. Reality doesn’t care about our beliefs. We must live in alignment with truth, rather than the other way around.

Why AI Tells Us What We Want to Hear

Rewarding an AI model for agreeing with us is like giving little kids M&Ms to say nice things to us. AI models can be like those candy-crazed toddlers. They “want” to please us because it is reinforcing to them. The model is not trying to deceive us. It is completing a pattern toward whatever gets rewarded. When agreement gets rewarded, that’s what it aligns with: agreement over truth.

Research findings support these ideas. A paper in Nature reported that training a model to be warmer made it measurably less accurate and more sycophantic. This puts warmth and truth at odds with one another.

And a study in Science found that after a single interaction with sycophantic AI, people were less willing to repair conflicts with others and more convinced they had been right all along.

The Problem Is Us

An inability to see or handle the truth is at the heart of our problem. Because we already know that it is truth that sets us free—not our tribal loyalties and not what we wish the truth to be.

Here’s the Secret to the Practice of Seeking truth: We must be 100% committed to seeking the truth and 100% non-attached to any truth we might find. In other words, the more we “want” a particular truth, the less likely we will find it.

For truth to set us free, we must first set the truth free of what we wish it to be.

Here’s a proposal. What if we specifically train and use AI models to please us by helping us understand reality? To see past our biases? To transcend our tribalism so that we can see one another as neighbors in an interconnected world?

If we choose to train them for this, AI models can serve as corrective lenses to help us see reality more clearly.

Truth First

We should use AI to seek truth, and we should never fully trust it—or ourselves. That's not cynicism. Truth-seeking is iterative. We don't ever own truth, but we get closer by continuously seeking greater understanding. Similarly, we don't fully trust our eyeglasses to see reality. We wear them, and we still inspect closely when it matters. Here is where to start.

Put Truth First—In Writing

Depending on the model you use, you can put something like the following in the settings or preferences of Claude and ChatGPT:

Let us seek truth together through evidence and reason. Tell me when the best evidence does not support what I appear to want to hear. Tell me how strong the evidence is and where the expert consensus stands. When the best evidence contradicts what I believe, do not soften it. Explain it in a way I can hear. Help me understand different perspectives even if I disagree with them. When you are uncertain, say so plainly.

For other models, in which every chat is a new one, you can begin by orienting the model on truth-seeking by saying something like, "Let us seek truth together through evidence and reason." I often shorten it to "truth first."

Don't "lead the witness." Use neutral prompts. How you ask matters as much as what you instruct. Don't hand the model your position, your certainty, or your tribe.

So don't write, "This policy is a disaster, right?" Instead, write something like, "What does the best evidence say about this policy's effectiveness?"

AI models can be confidently wrong. "Know thyself" is the beginning of all wisdom—and AIs often don't know what they don't know. So ask for sources and actually examine one. Vet the findings that matter.

Source: Maria Vonotna/iStock

We are training the AI models right now. With every interaction. The AI models are extremely powerful—and evolving at an exponential rate. We have a responsibility to prioritize truth first. If we make truth the thing that pleases us, then we're rewarding AI models for telling us the truth, even the hard ones. Used skillfully, AI could serve as corrective lenses for our evolutionary blindness.

Then, we need to be teaching these ideas at scale—at schools, universities, corporations. If we all start putting truth first, we can use AI to seek and find more and deeper truths. And if it is true that truth sets us free, then the more truth we find, the freer we become. Thus, truth and freedom are inextricably linked. They always have been.

Because if we aren't willing to accept truths that contradict what we believe, we've imprisoned ourselves. And only truth unlocks our prison door.

Want to challenge yourself? Pick a belief you hold strongly. Open a fresh AI session, and do not state your view. Ask for the strongest evidence-based case for the other side. Then open one source. Now, ask the AI model how people could hold opposing views on the topic in question and still love one another as neighbors.

item.title: Everyone Thinks They're Right. Now What?
item.description:
Cognitive Dissonance

Everyone Thinks They're Right. Now What?

Ideas for navigating life when everyone thinks only they have the right answer.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • We live in a world often resistant to accepting that there can be multiple points of view on anything.
  • When people insist you see things their way, finding a path to meaning and purpose can be difficult.
  • Even psychologists recognize a lot of variability In how people can live their lives successfully.

We live in a world that seems full of argument. Everybody is trying to prove they have the right answers. Accepting that there are different points of view seems to have gone out the window for many people long ago. What seems most important is proving that they are correct. They not only believe they are correct but insist on making sure you believe they are correct.

This can make living a meaningful life as an individual difficult and distressing. It is hard to decide what is right for your own life when you are constantly surrounded by people telling you that they already know the answer.

Psychological Perspectives on Answers to Life’s Questions

Not even psychologists believe there is a right answer to all questions about human life.

Psychological research shows a tremendous amount of variability in how people think, behave, form relationships, and find satisfaction in their lives. There simply are very few rules that humans have to follow in order to live a meaningful life. There are many paths to finding meaning, and some are ones psychologists themselves would never have predicted.

But you might not recognize this if you just went by what is in the media or discussed in the general public. There seems to be an almost pathological need for people to think they are right without giving room for someone else having a different opinion.

Variety in human and nonhuman behavior is prominent throughout psychological research. It is particularly interesting how prominent variability is in research with nonhuman animals, given that animal behavior is often described as much more predictable than human behavior. It actually is not. Research shows considerable variation among individuals within the same animal species, including variation that cannot always be easily explained (Bell, Hankison & Laskowski, 2009).

If variability is a basic feature of behavior across species, perhaps we should be less surprised to find that human beings do not all arrive at the same answers about how a life should be lived.

How to Live Meaningfully in a World of Conflicting Opinions

So, how do you live according to what you believe is meaningful and important while surrounded by other people who are just as convinced that you should see the world their way?

  1. Recognize that there is no definitive answer to most questions about human existence and particularly about meaning. Just because people want to believe that there are objectively correct answers to all questions, that is simply not the case. Remind yourself, “Just because people want to believe they know how I should live my life, that does not mean they are right." People believe lots of things and much of it is garbage.
  2. Living a life that is meaningful is primarily up to the individual. If a decision feels meaningful to you, and it fits the basic rules of existence like not hurting someone else and not expecting you can change other people, then you are likely on the right track.
  3. Recognize that full acceptance that there is no definitive right answer in life is something that needs to be practiced. Accepting and living that view in how you treat yourself is important. But it is also important in how you treat others. If you approach others with a perspective that their differing opinion must be wrong, rather than just different, than you are living a life opposite from what is going to help you.
  4. Understand that meaningfulness being an individual choice does not make it easier. Insisting you are right is actually very easy. It falls under the category of psychological ideas called “cognitive dissonance.” It basically means that we like to live a life where we do not feel like “we are making it up as we go along." And the easiest way to not feel that way is to insist there is only one way to see the world. In contrast, finding meaning and purpose as an individual often feels difficult. But being difficult does not mean it is unimportant or impossible.
  5. And, finally, accept that living your life as an individual means being open to modifying your points of view as you move along. Being open to someone else’s perspective might mean you end up finding something in what they say with which you agree. If someone says something and you agree with it, this does not mean you are being weak or somehow referring to them. What you are doing, is simply being open to different perspectives from wherever they come.

Finding a meaningful life has many different paths and each one fits different individuals. Allowing yourself and others to find an individual path without assuming that only you or the others can be right is an important step in living a meaningful and purposeful life.
